A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same tokenization framework and provide readable text, equations, proofs, diagrams, and worked examples. Both end with references; neither contains an appendix. The material supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 presents mathematical definitions, proofs, and constructed examples in Sections 3–5. Empirical findings are attributed to prior work; no original experiments, simulations, or data analyses are reported.

after.justification: v3 remains a theoretical paper. Its added proposition and expanded discussion do not introduce original empirical results, and Section 7 continues to describe experimental investigation as future work.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the tokenizer as a pair of stochastic encoder and decoder maps and the same distribution-mapping framework. The revised formal properties and proofs do not introduce a new tokenization algorithm, architecture, objective, or inference procedure.

E1.justification: Neither version trains or evaluates on datasets or benchmarks. The constructed alphabet and tokenization examples are retained; newly cited empirical studies do not constitute additional task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods against a proposed implementation. BPE, WordPiece, and Unigram remain theoretical illustrations, while additional cited methods serve the literature discussion.

E3.justification: Neither version specifies an original experimental evaluation protocol. No splits, evaluation metrics, training budgets, model configurations, or testing procedures are added or revised.

E4.justification: The inconsistency, ambiguity, and uncomputability examples in Examples 4.1, 4.2, and 5.1 are retained. Neither version contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, or error analyses; the added normalization discussion is conceptual.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. The mathematical treatment of estimator consistency is not empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: There are no original empirical result entries in either version. Figure 1 retains the reference probabilities (0.2, 0.4, 0.4), encoded probabilities (0.2, 0, 0.8), and decoded probabilities (0, 0.2, 0.8). The other worked examples retain their findings.

T1.justification: v3 makes substantive repairs to the mathematical foundation: Lemma 3.1 corrects the sign in its Fatou argument, and Lemma 3.2 restores a limit and replaces an equality with the required inequality. Section 2 adds definitions of stochastic-map support, injectivity, and surjectivity. New Proposition 3.2 proves decoder determinism on the encoder's support, qualifying v1's unrestricted assertion. Theorem 3.1 itself is unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: a stochastic-map framework, necessary and sufficient conditions for preserving estimator consistency, and analysis of statistical and computational concerns. The revised motivation and emphasis on representation learning do not change these core claims.

C2.justification: Section 4 adds explanations connecting normalization operations to noninjective encoding and discusses stochastic decoding as a possible approach to unfamiliar symbols. Section 7 newly acknowledges that effective computation of exact tokenizers remains unaddressed. These refine practical implications and limitations within the retained theoretical scope.

D1.justification: No implementation, experimental hyperparameters, hardware specifications, training times, or code/data release information for this work is added or revised. The new references to tokenizer software and preprocessing operations support conceptual discussion rather than reproducibility instructions.

R1.justification: v3 replaces the extensive historical-linguistic positioning around Plato, Saussure, and Chomsky with a substantially expanded contemporary NLP context. It adds discussion and citations covering token-free models, empirical tokenizer studies, open-vocabulary approaches, and marginalization methods. Section 4 replaces the detailed Cao and Rimell discussion with a broader set of related approaches.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten, and the historical opening and Saussure epigraph are removed. Sections 4–5 gain topical paragraph headings, expanded explanations, and more explicit encoder/decoder terminology. The main section sequence remains stable, but the narrative is substantially refocused.

P2.justification: v3 redesigns the title and author block, adds running Preprint headers and rules, changes heading typography, and adjusts spacing and figure placement relative to the text. Figure 1 and the existing commutative diagrams remain; no new tables or substantive graphical displays are introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 improves mathematical reliability through the corrections to Lemmas 3.1–3.2 and the qualified determinism proof in Proposition 3.2. Its focused introduction and explicit computational limitation also improve clarity. The gains remain limited: the central theorem and examples are unchanged, and Definition 4.1 still asserts decoder determinism more broadly than Proposition 3.2 establishes.
